summary: An April 1st humor RFC about encapsulating IP datagrams on top of what it calls Acoustical Transmission Media, a pun on the real ATM networking technology. It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke about sending network messages as sounds, using the same three letters as a real technology. It was written for April Fools Day.

questions: is there a joke rfc about atm
subtitle: An April Fools joke about transmitting IP datagrams over sound waves

tldr.problem: Laptops have audio hardware but no standard for sending IP packets over sound.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC (published April 1, 1996) proposes encapsulating IP datagrams as Morse code transmitted via sound waves at different frequencies (440 Hz to 784 Hz) to create separate Local Acoustical Networks (LANs).
tldr.outcome: A clever pun playing on the acronym ATM (normally Asynchronous Transfer Mode), reinterpreted as Acoustical Transmission Media.

today: RFC 1926 is Informational and exists as a historical artifact of IETF April Fools traditions. No implementation was ever created. The real ATM technology (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) continued as a legitimate networking standard.

sections.title: The Setup
sections.content:
This RFC is an April Fools joke, published on 1 April 1996. It proposes a method of encapsulating IP datagrams on top of Acoustical Transmission Media (ATM), a clever pun on the real networking standard Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM). The joke hinges on the observation that laptops have audio hardware that could theoretically transmit data as sound.

The proposal is presented in deadpan technical language, complete with a frame format, modulation scheme, frequency assignments, and security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a silly April Fools joke pretending you can send Internet data by making beeping sounds, using the same letters as a real networking technology.

sections.title: The Encoding Scheme
sections.content:
The IP datagram is divided into 4-bit chunks and converted to characters using a 16-character table (each bit pattern from 0000 to 1111 maps to a letter like 'i', 't', 's', 'a', etc.). A single 'b' character is prepended as a frame start signal. The characters are then transmitted in Morse code by modulating a steady tone on and off at one of seven standard frequencies: 440 Hz (a), 494 Hz (b), 523 Hz (c), 587 Hz (d), 659 Hz (e), 698 Hz (f), or 784 Hz (g).

Different frequencies represent different Local Acoustical Networks (LANs). The default AS (Acoustical Signature) number is 'a', at 440 Hz. Reception is simply the reverse process.
sections.plainLanguage: Convert each bit of the data to a letter, send that letter as Morse code in sound form at a certain pitch, and different pitches mean different networks.

sections.title: Why This Is Funny
sections.content:
The RFC is funny because it takes a ridiculous premise (networking over beeping) and treats it with complete technical seriousness. It includes proper sections (Overview, Frame transmission, Frame reception, Security Considerations), standard frequency assignments, and even practical advice (users should take precautions in crowded areas).

The author's email address at the end is signed in actual Morse code, a final touch to the punchline. The RFC exists in the formal IETF archive as a historical artifact of April Fools humor.
sections.plainLanguage: It's funny because it's written like a serious technical document about something absurd—sending network data as beeping sounds.
